section.title: The Garden of Union
section.sectionRationale: This is the summit and center of the Song. The bridegroom praises his bride from head to foot, calls her his sister, his bride, altogether beautiful with no flaw, and names her a garden locked and a fountain sealed. She invites him into his garden, and he comes, and the friends bless the union. The movement celebrates the consummation of covenant love with reverence and joy.
section.thesis: Covenant love reaches its consummation: the bridegroom delights in his bride as altogether beautiful and flawless, honors her as a garden kept for him alone, and enters at her invitation, while the friends bless the union of the two made one.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the bridegroom’s praise of his flawless bride and his call to come away with him; the bride as a garden locked and a fountain sealed, opened only to her beloved; and the coming into the garden, sealed by the friends’ blessing, eat and drink, O beloved.

verses.text: How beautiful you are, my {{raya|darling}}, how very beautiful! Your eyes are like doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats streaming down Mount Gilead.
Your teeth are like a flock of newly shorn sheep coming up from the washing; each has its twin, and not one of them is lost.
Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your mouth is lovely. Your brow behind your veil is like a slice of pomegranate.
Your neck is like the tower of David, built with rows of stones; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors.
Your breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle grazing among the lilies.
Before the day breaks and the shadows flee, I will make my way to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense.
You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw.

units.label: A garden locked, a fountain sealed

verses.text: Come with me from Lebanon, my {{kallah|bride}}, come with me from Lebanon! Descend from the peak of Amana, from the summits of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of the lions, from the mountains of the leopards.
You have captured my heart, my sister, my bride; you have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your neck.
How delightful is your {{ahavah|love}}, my sister, my bride! Your love is much better than wine, and the fragrance of your perfume than all spices.
Your lips, my bride, drip sweetness like the honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue, and the fragrance of your garments is like the aroma of Lebanon.
My sister, my bride, you are a {{gan|garden}} locked up, a spring enclosed, a fountain sealed.
Your branches are an orchard of pomegranates with the choicest of fruits, with henna and nard,
with nard and saffron, with calamus and cinnamon, with every kind of frankincense tree, with myrrh and aloes, with all the finest spices.
You are a garden spring, a well of fresh water flowing down from Lebanon.

units.label: Into the garden, and the blessing

verses.text: Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind. Breathe on my garden and spread the fragrance of its spices. Let my beloved come into his garden and taste its choicest fruits.

I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice. I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved.

raya.gloss: My darling, literally my companion or dear friend, the bridegroom’s recurring name for the bride. Here it opens his praise: how beautiful you are, my darling.

kallah.gloss: Bride. In this movement the man calls the woman my sister, my bride, language of covenant nearness and pure delight; she is family and beloved, wholly his by covenant.

ahavah.gloss: Love. Here the bride’s love is declared much better than wine; the same word that crowns the Song at 8:6, covenant love, delighted in and returned.

gan.gloss: Garden. The bride is a garden locked and a fountain sealed, opened only to her beloved. The garden imagery recalls Eden and pictures faithful, exclusive love as a place of life, fruitfulness, and delight.

basic.context: This is the high point at the center of the Song, the wedding night. The bridegroom praises his bride from head to foot, calling her altogether beautiful, with no flaw. He names her his sister, his bride, and a garden locked, a fountain sealed, kept for him alone. She invites him in, he comes to his garden, and the friends give their blessing. It is the consummation of covenant love, celebrated with reverence and joy.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a wedding song, and it treats the union of husband and wife as pure and good, not shameful. The praise is poetic and modest in its imagery. On the plain level it honors the intimacy of marriage as God’s good gift. Within the whole Bible, the flawless bride and the sealed garden opened to the beloved point to Christ and the church, a bride made spotless and belonging wholly to Him.
basic.originalLanguages: The man calls the woman raya, my darling, and kallah, my bride, joined with my sister, words of covenant nearness. Her love is ahavah, better than wine. Above all she is a gan, a garden, locked and sealed, opened only to her beloved, an image of faithful, exclusive love that recalls Eden.
basic.typology: The bride who is altogether beautiful with no flaw pictures the church that Christ presents to Himself radiant, without spot or wrinkle. The garden locked and then joyfully opened to the beloved pictures love kept faithful and then fully given within covenant.
basic.christ: You are altogether beautiful, no flaw in you, the bridegroom says, and Paul says Christ gave Himself for the church to present her without blemish. The bride flawless in her beloved’s eyes is the church made spotless in Christ. The union blessed by the friends anticipates the joy of Christ and His people made one.
basic.god: God is the author of marriage and of its intimacy, and He calls it good and beautiful, not unclean. He is not embarrassed by the delight of husband and wife but blesses it. And He is preparing a bride for His Son, whom He will make flawless and bring home.
basic.crossReferences: Ephesians 5:25 to 27, Christ presents the church without spot or wrinkle. Genesis 2:24 to 25, the one flesh union without shame. Revelation 21:2, the bride adorned for her husband.
basic.oneStory: The garden of union celebrates covenant love brought to its joyful consummation. It honors the goodness of marriage and points beyond it to Christ, who makes His bride flawless and delights to make her His own.

context.literary:
This is the Song's longest sustained poem and its midpoint, and it has the shape of a slow approach. The first movement, 4:1-7, is a descriptive praise poem, often called by its Arabic name, a wasf. It moves downward from the eyes and hair to the teeth, lips, brow, neck and breasts, and it is bracketed by two near-identical lines, 'How beautiful you are, my darling' at the start and 'You are altogether beautiful' at the close. In the middle, in verse 6, the speaker interrupts his own praise with a vow to go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense before the shadows flee.

The second movement, 4:8-15, shifts from the body to the landscape. The title 'bride' now fills every verse from 4:9 to 4:12, and the images move from animals and towers to a garden, a spring and a well. The woman has become a place, and the place is closed. The movement ends with a rising list of spices, each more exotic than the last, so that the reader is brought to the garden gate with all senses awake.

The third movement, 4:16 to 5:1, is a short exchange that carries the whole weight of the book. For the first time in the chapter she speaks, calling on the winds to wake her garden and inviting him in, and notably she calls it 'his garden'. He answers at once, 'I have come to my garden,' and now it is 'my garden'. The shift from her gift to his possession is the poem's quiet climax. The final line is spoken by neither lover, and the chapter closes with an invitation to eat and drink. The chapter break, which places 5:1 in chapter 5, hides how tightly it belongs to the scene before it.
context.historical:
The images in the praise poem are taken from the world the first hearers knew. Black goats on the slopes of Gilead, east of the Jordan, looked from a distance like dark hair rippling down the hillside. Sheep that had just been shorn and washed were clean and white, and an even set of paired teeth is imagined as a flock in which every ewe has her twin and none is bereaved. A tower hung with shields, as in Ezekiel 27:10-11 where mercenaries hung their shields on Tyre's walls, was a sign of splendor and strength, and a scarlet ribbon and a split pomegranate were familiar colours of the market and the orchard.

The call in verse 8 names the northern heights: Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon. Deuteronomy 3:9 tells us that Senir is the Amorite name for Hermon. These are wild, remote peaks, the dens of lions and leopards, and the image of descending from them to a garden is the image of coming out of danger into safety.

The garden itself belongs to a royal world. Walled gardens with sealed springs were a luxury in a dry land, and the royal speaker of Ecclesiastes 2:5 says that he made gardens and parks and planted fruit trees. The spices of 4:13-14 are imported, such as nard, cinnamon and aloes, and their presence here makes the garden a picture of wealth as much as beauty.

The setting is a wedding. In Israel the wedding celebration could last several days, Genesis 29:27, and the bridegroom had companions, Judges 14:11 and John 3:29, who are the 'friends' addressed at the end of 5:1. The use of 'sister' as a term of love is also found in the love poetry of the surrounding cultures, where it carries intimacy and equality, not blood relation.
context.canonical:
The Song's garden stands in conscious relation to Eden. Genesis 2:8-9 describes a garden planted by God with every tree pleasing to the eye, and Genesis 2:25 ends with a man and woman naked and unashamed. Genesis 3 loses both the garden and the innocence. In Song 4 a man and a woman again stand in a garden, again without shame, and the poem draws its imagery from the same stock of fruit, water and spice. This does not mean the Song undoes the fall, but it shows that the original goodness of marriage survives the fall as a gift that can be received with joy.

Proverbs 5:15-19 is the nearest neighbour. The father tells his son to drink from his own cistern, to let his fountain be blessed, and to rejoice in the wife of his youth, and the fountain, spring and fawn imagery overlap with Song 4. The same water language that warns against infidelity in Proverbs here celebrates faithful union.

The prophets use the garden as a promise. Isaiah 51:3 says that the Lord will make Zion's wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD, and Isaiah 58:11 speaks of a well-watered garden. The New Testament carries the pattern forward in two ways. Paul says that Christ gave Himself for the church to present her without stain or wrinkle, Ephesians 5:25-27, and then quotes Genesis 2:24 and calls marriage a profound mystery pointing to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. And in Revelation 22:1-2 the garden returns as a city with a river and a tree of life.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet means to teach a people that desire is not an enemy to be feared, and not a toy to be used, but a garden to be tended and given at the right time. The first hearers lived among neighbours who treated sexuality as a power to be appeased or a pleasure to be taken. The poem answers with a picture of a husband who praises, waits, calls, and is invited, and of a wife who both guards her garden and opens it by her own choice.

The text also teaches by its restraint. It speaks in images, never in anatomy. The body is described through fawns, fruit, perfume and spring water, and when the union arrives in 5:1 it is covered by the words 'I have come to my garden' and a blessing from the friends. The first hearers are taught that intimacy is honorable enough to be spoken of with dignity.

The poet also wants them to notice the order of things. Praise comes first, then the invitation to leave the dangerous heights, then the garden's closed gate, then her invitation, then the union. The movement shows what love must be like before its consummation: admiring, patient and given freely.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This section records one couple's wedding night, and it is not a manual. The images are the poet's own, and no reader is expected to copy them or measure a spouse against them. The praise belongs to this man and woman and to their culture's imagination.

Even so, some things in the passage reach beyond the couple. The garden is locked and sealed until it is opened by invitation, which is why the passage is a fitting companion to Hebrews 13:4, which says that marriage is to be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled. Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 7:3-5 on mutual giving between husband and wife stand in the same line. The passage prescribes nothing but implies much: that intimacy belongs inside covenant, that it is given and not seized, and that it is meant to be glad.

It also needs care in pastoral use. A passage that praises a bride as flawless can become a weight on those whose marriages have been marked by sin or wounds. The better application is to see it as God's picture of what marriage is for and to bring even the broken places to the One who makes all things new.

debates.question: What kind of book is the Song: a celebration of married love, an allegory of Christ and the church, or both?

views.label: A celebration of covenant married love
views.case: This central movement plainly celebrates the intimacy of husband and wife on their wedding night, honoring it as good and pure; Scripture openly commends such delight within marriage, Genesis 2:24 to 25 and Proverbs 5.

views.label: An allegory of Christ and the church, or God and Israel
views.case: The church has long read the flawless bride and the garden opened to the beloved as Christ and His spotless church, in keeping with Ephesians 5:25 to 27 and the Bible’s marriage covenant, and has been wary of dwelling only on the literal.

views.label: Both, the literal union as a God-given sign
views.case: The wisest reading holds both: the poem truly celebrates the good gift of marital union, and because that union is a God-given sign of Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31 to 32, the flawless bride and sealed garden rightly point to the church made spotless in Christ.

debates.bearing: Holding both keeps the passage reverent and honest: it neither treats married intimacy as shameful nor spiritualizes it away, but honors the gift and follows it to Christ, who makes His bride without flaw.

debates.question: What does the sealed garden mean: bodily purity, exclusive fidelity, or the wife's own consent?

views.label: Her virginity before marriage
views.case: A locked garden and sealed spring are things no one has entered. Many interpreters hear a reference to the bride's purity on the wedding night, in line with the Old Testament's regard for virginity at marriage.

views.label: Exclusive faithfulness to him alone
views.case: The image of a closed spring echoes Proverbs 5:15-17, where the fountain is to be 'yours alone, never to be shared with strangers.' On this reading the emphasis falls on marital fidelity, which applies to husband and wife alike.

views.label: Her freedom to give herself
views.case: The garden is locked, and her own words in 4:16 invite him in. The lock is hers to open, so the image honors her consent and agency, and nothing in the poem is taken from her.

debates.bearing: The three readings are not rivals. The image holds purity, fidelity and consent together, and the movement of the poem from 'locked' to 'come into his garden' shows love that is guarded until it is given.

debates.question: Who speaks the last line of 5:1, 'Eat, O friends, and drink'?

views.label: The bridegroom
views.case: The verse begins with him and continues in his voice, so the final call is his invitation to the wedding guests to share in the joy of the day.

views.label: The chorus of friends or the poet
views.case: The address to 'friends' and 'beloved' looks like a different voice commenting on the union, blessing it, and drawing the reader into the feast.

views.label: God as the approving voice
views.case: Some interpreters have heard here the approval of God Himself on marital union, noting that nothing else in the poem is said to the lovers after the union. The text does not name God, so this is an inference.

debates.bearing: The text does not identify the speaker, and the poem's reserve is itself a lesson. A blessing is given and the door is closed to the reader, so that the scene is honored and not exposed.

study.originalLanguages:
The first praise is said of her eyes: 'doves behind your veil'. The word for veil is the one used of a woman's covering in other settings, and the picture is of a gaze glimpsed, not displayed. In verse 2 the teeth are paired, 'each has its twin', and 'not one of them is lost.' The Hebrew word behind 'lost' comes from the root for being bereaved of children, the word Jacob uses of himself when he fears losing his sons, Genesis 42:36. In the poem it means that every tooth has its partner and none is missing. The tower of verse 4 is built with a rare word of uncertain meaning, usually taken as rows or courses of stones, and its precise sense cannot be recovered with confidence.

In verse 9, 'you have captured my heart' is a verb formed from the noun for heart, so it means something like 'you have heart-ed me', a verb the poet apparently forged to say what ordinary language could not. In verse 10 the Hebrew word for love is the plural word for lovemaking and caresses, as in Proverbs 7:18, so the poet is saying that her lovemaking is better than wine.

Verse 12 uses two verbs of closure. The first means to lock, as in Judges 3:23 where Ehud locks the doors of the upper room, and the second means to seal with a signet, as in Jeremiah 32:10 where Jeremiah signs and seals the deed. The garden is therefore both bolted and stamped, as property is sealed by its owner. The word for 'spring' in verse 12 is unusual in its form, which is why translations differ over the exact phrase.

Verse 13 describes her as an 'orchard', a word that gives us the English word paradise. It is a loanword of foreign origin, found only three times in the Old Testament, here, in Ecclesiastes 2:5 and in Nehemiah 2:8, and the Greek translation of Genesis uses the corresponding Greek word for the garden of Eden. The reader is invited to hear Eden in the spice-filled orchard.

Finally, in verse 6 the poem repeats a line from 2:17, 'Before the day breaks and the shadows flee,' but now the man says it. What was her invitation to him in chapter 2 becomes his vow to her, and the word for myrrh, the poem's signature spice, returns at 4:6, 4:14 and 5:1, tying the mountain, the garden and the feast together.

typology.fulfillment: The bridegroom's verdict is spoken before any of her beauty is earned. Paul says that Christ gave Himself up for the church to cleanse her and present her to Himself as glorious, 'without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless,' Ephesians 5:25-27. Ezekiel 16:14 describes the same gift, a beauty made 'perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you.' The correspondence is that the Bridegroom praises what He has made beautiful. The type falls short because the Song's bride is praised for what she is, while the church is made what she is by the cost of His blood.

typology.type: Called down from the lions' dens, 4:8
typology.fulfillment: The bridegroom summons the bride from the dangerous northern heights, from lions and leopards. In the New Testament this becomes the rescue of the church: God 'has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son,' Colossians 1:13. The type shows love as an act of descent and invitation, and the church is lifted from danger into belonging. It falls short because the bride of the Song only needs to leave a mountain, whereas the church is delivered from death.

typology.type: The garden entered and enjoyed, 4:16 to 5:1
typology.fulfillment: The garden opened to the beloved is a picture of a people in whom the Lord takes delight. Isaiah 51:3 says that God will make Zion's wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD, and John sets key moments of the gospel in gardens, John 18:1 and 19:41. The Song's garden gives the church language for the fruit she bears for Christ. The type falls short because the garden of the Song is guarded by a bride's own love, whereas the church's fruit is the work of the Spirit.

The meal of honey, wine and milk shared by the friends is a picture of the feast that the Lord promises. At the last supper Jesus said that He would not drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when He drinks it anew with His people in His Father's kingdom, Matthew 26:29, and Revelation 19:9 pronounces blessed those invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb. The type falls short because the Song's feast is a night's celebration, while the supper of the Lamb is the joy of the age to come.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most plainly through Paul's use of marriage. In Ephesians 5 the apostle moves from the husband's duty to the work of Christ: He loved the church, gave Himself up for her, cleansed her by the washing with water through the word, and presents her to Himself without stain or wrinkle, 5:25-27. He then quotes the creation text about leaving and cleaving and says 'This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church,' 5:31-32. A reader who takes Paul at his word does not need to force the Song into allegory. The relationship that the poem celebrates is a created sign of the one that Christ has with His people.

The words of the bridegroom in verse 7 take on a new weight in that light. A man who says 'there is no flaw in you' to a bride who has sinned seems either blind or generous. The gospel says that Christ's generosity is real: the verdict He gives is true because He has made it true. He bore the stain Himself and has cleansed her. The words 'you have captured my heart' point to the love that brought Him down from heaven, and Zephaniah 3:17 gives the same picture of God who rejoices over His people with singing.

The call from the mountains of lions in verse 8 can be heard as His voice calling His people out of the dominion of darkness, Colossians 1:13, and the invitation of verse 16 as the church's answer. The Song gives her words to say: 'Let my beloved come into his garden.' The believing heart is not a fortress to be stormed but a garden given freely to its rightful Lord.

The garden also reminds us of Christ's own gardens: the one where He prayed before His arrest, John 18:1, and the one with a new tomb where no one had yet been laid, John 19:41. Mary mistakes Him for the gardener, John 20:15, and the reader may recall that the first garden was lost by the first Adam and found again by the last. This is a pattern, not an allegory of the Song's text, and it should be held loosely.

What the Song does not do is assign each limb of the bride a doctrine. The hair, the teeth and the neck are the poet's tributes to a particular woman and carry no hidden meaning. What reaches Christ is the shape of the whole: a bridegroom who praises, a bride who gives, a union that is blessed, and a feast that follows.
study.god:
This section shows a God who made delight and is not embarrassed by it. The Song is a book in the canon, and its centre is a wedding night spoken of with reverence. That alone tells us something about the Lord: He blessed the first man and woman and told them to be fruitful, Genesis 1:28, and He saw that marriage was good before sin entered. The Bible does not treat the body as a problem to be solved. Hebrews 13:4 says that marriage should be honored by all and the marriage bed kept undefiled, and that holds the same two truths together that the Song's garden does: delight and boundary.

The poem also shows God as jealous for faithfulness. A garden that is locked and a spring that is sealed speak of something owned and guarded. Exodus 34:14 says that the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God, and Hosea 2:19-20 has Him promise to betroth His people forever in righteousness, justice, loving devotion, compassion and faithfulness. The sealed garden does not diminish God's generosity; it shows that His love is committed and not casual.

There is a tension here that the passage holds without strain. God is holy, and He is also glad, and He lets the language of bodily love serve as a picture of His own relation to His people. The One who is high above all is also the Bridegroom who delights. Zephaniah 3:17 says that He will rejoice over His people with gladness and quiet them with His love.

God is also shown as the one who makes beautiful. The bridegroom's praise of the bride's beauty mirrors Ezekiel 16, where the Lord finds a helpless girl, covers her, bathes and clothes her, and her fame spreads because her beauty was perfect in the splendor He bestowed, 16:8-14. His praise does not flatter; it names what His love has made.

For worship this means thankfulness for the physical and domestic good of life, and fidelity in the places where we are tempted to treat love cheaply. It also means joy in being delighted in. The believer does not come to God as a servant approved with reluctance but as one He has taken as His own, and the closing call to 'eat and drink' belongs to that gladness.

crossReferences.note: God plants a garden with trees that are pleasing to the eye and good for food, and the Song's garden of fruit, spice and water draws on the same pattern. The echo invites the reader to hear Eden's goodness in the lovers' garden, before the fall closed it.

The first marriage: a man leaves his parents, is united to his wife, and the two are naked and not ashamed. Song 4 is a poem in which that unashamed union is described and honored, and the Song's wedding night returns the reader to the first marriage.

A father urges his son to drink from his own cistern and rejoice in the wife of his youth, using fountain, spring and doe imagery that overlaps with Song 4. The same water language warns against faithlessness and celebrates faithfulness.

The adulteress offers 'loving caresses' using the same plural word for love that Song 4:10 praises as better than wine. Set side by side, they show the same desire in two settings, one stolen and one covenanted, with very different ends.

Christ gave Himself for the church to present her without stain or wrinkle, holy and blameless. This is the clearest New Testament key to the bridegroom's words in Song 4:7, and shows that the flawless bride is made so by His work.

Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says the mystery of marriage points to Christ and the church. It gives the apostolic warrant for hearing the Song's wedding night as both a real marriage and a sign of a greater union.

The Lord covers an abandoned girl, pledges Himself to her, bathes and adorns her, and her beauty is perfect in the splendor He bestowed. It is a prophetic parallel to the bridegroom's praise, showing that a beloved's beauty can be a gift of the lover.

The Lord will make Zion's wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD. The promise takes the garden image of the Song and sets it on the horizon of God's restoration of His people.

Marriage is to be honored and its bed kept undefiled. The verse draws the practical line from the poem's celebration: intimacy is good and is to be kept in covenant, which is the lock and seal of the Song's garden.

Husband and wife are to give to each other and not to deprive one another, because each has authority over the other's body. It shares the Song's mutuality, in which she invites him and he receives, and neither takes.

A river of the water of life and the tree of life stand in the new city. The garden's spring and fruit return in the final vision, so that the lost garden of Genesis and the garden of the Song find their completion.

The bride says 'Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved.' In 4:6 the bridegroom takes up her words and makes them his vow, so that the longing of chapter 2 has become the shared purpose of chapter 4.

study.oneStory:
This is the poem where the Bible's story of the garden is told at the scale of two people. In creation God plants a garden, makes a man and a woman, and sees that it is very good. The union of the two, naked and unashamed, is the crown of that world, Genesis 2:24-25. Song 4 is the clearest place after Genesis where a man and woman again stand in a garden, in love, and in joy.

The fall broke that joy, and the shame, blame and domination of Genesis 3:7, 12, 16 entered even the closest of relationships. The Old Testament does not pretend otherwise: marriages are fractured by polygamy, adultery and abuse, and the prophets use the image of an unfaithful wife for Israel's idolatry. Against that background, the Song stands out as a witness that the original goodness has not been lost altogether. It is a place where the garden can be glimpsed again, inside a marriage kept faithful.

The redemption story gives the garden a deeper meaning. Isaiah promises that God will make Zion's desert like the garden of the LORD, Isaiah 51:3, and Ezekiel 16 pictures the Lord Himself finding His people, covering their nakedness and adorning them. The New Testament says what the Song hints: Christ loves the church and gave Himself up for her to present her without stain or wrinkle, Ephesians 5:25-27, and marriage is a mystery pointing to that union, Ephesians 5:31-32. The garden where Christ prayed and the garden where He was buried are the places where He faced the cost of that love.

The new creation closes the circle. The holy city comes down 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2, and the river of the water of life and the tree of life stand within it, Revelation 22:1-2. The garden of Eden, the sealed garden of the Song and the city of Revelation belong to one story. The bridegroom who called his bride down from the lions' dens will bring His people home to a garden that is never shut again, and the invitation to eat and drink will be spoken over the whole redeemed people.

quiz.q: What does the bridegroom declare about his bride in 4:7?

options.text: You are altogether beautiful, my darling; in you there is no flaw.
options.note: This verdict is the pivot of the movement and echoes Ephesians 5.

options.text: You are beautiful, though many flaws remain to be fixed.
options.note: He does call her beautiful, but he goes further and declares her without flaw, wholly delighted in her, leaving no blemish to be fixed.

options.text: You must become beautiful before I will love you.
options.note: He does prize her beauty, but he loves and delights in her as she is, calling her flawless; his love does not wait for her to become beautiful.

options.text: Your beauty is fading with age.
options.note: He praises her beauty without reserve, seeing no flaw.

quiz.q: What does the image of a garden locked and a fountain sealed picture in 4:12?

options.text: Love kept faithful and reserved for the beloved alone, then joyfully given within covenant.
options.note: The sealed garden pictures exclusive, faithful love opened only to the one beloved.

options.text: A love that is cold and permanently closed off.
options.note: It is truly sealed and closed to all others, but not cold or permanent; the garden is joyfully opened to the beloved, 4:16 to 5:1.

options.text: A literal garden the bride owns.
options.note: It does use the picture of a garden, but the garden is an image of the bride herself, kept for her beloved, not a literal plot she owns.

options.text: A warning against marriage.
options.note: It honors faithful marital love, not a warning against it.

quiz.q: What does the man call the woman throughout this movement?

options.text: My sister, my bride, words of covenant nearness and pure delight.
options.note: Sister and bride together signal family closeness and covenant love.

options.text: A passing acquaintance.
options.note: He calls her my sister, my bride, the language of deep covenant belonging.

options.text: A servant in his household.
options.note: He does draw her into his household intimacy, but he honors her as his bride and equal in love, not as a servant.

options.text: A stranger from a far country.
options.note: He does call her from the heights of Lebanon, as from afar, but he names her his sister and his bride, deeply his own, not a stranger.

quiz.q: How does the flawless bride point to the gospel?

options.text: She pictures the church that Christ makes spotless and presents to Himself without blemish.
options.note: Ephesians 5 uses the same language of the church made radiant by Christ.

options.text: She teaches that only the sinless can be loved by God.
options.note: The verdict of no flaw is real, but the church is made flawless by her Beloved, not loved only because she is already sinless.

options.text: She shows that God finds fault with His bride.
options.note: The verdict is no flaw in you, the church beautiful in Christ.

options.text: She has no connection to Christ and the church.
options.note: She truly is a human bride called flawless, yet Scripture reads the spotless bride as a picture of the church made radiant by Christ, Ephesians 5:27, so she points beyond herself.

quiz.q: How does this movement treat the intimacy of marriage?

options.text: As a good, pure, and beautiful gift of God, celebrated with reverence and joy.
options.note: The Song honors marital union as good, not shameful.

options.text: As something shameful to be hidden and regretted.
options.note: The opposite: it is celebrated and blessed by the friends.

options.text: As unimportant and best ignored.
options.note: The Song does veil this intimacy in modest garden imagery, but it is far from unimportant; it stands at the center, honored as God’s good gift.

options.text: As permitted only reluctantly.
options.note: This intimacy is indeed permitted here, but far more than reluctantly; it is joyfully celebrated and blessed as God’s good gift.

questions: The bridegroom calls his bride altogether beautiful, with no flaw. How does it change you to hear that Christ sees His church, and you in Him, as beautiful and without blemish by His love?
The bride is a garden kept for her beloved alone. Where is God calling you to guard something faithful and reserved, whether in marriage, singleness, or your devotion to Him?
The Song treats marital intimacy as a good and holy gift, not something shameful. How does that shape the way you think and speak about the body and about marriage?
You have captured my heart, the bridegroom says over one glance. Have you considered that Christ delights in His people, and how might resting in His delight steady you today?
The friends bless the union with joy. How can you rejoice in and honor the marriages around you, and God’s good design for love, rather than treating them cynically?

translationNotes.note: The praise is a wasf, a poem describing the beloved’s beauty part by part; the images are evocative rather than literal likenesses.
A garden locked, a fountain sealed pictures love kept faithful and reserved for the one beloved.
The friends’ blessing, eat and drink, O beloved, closes the central movement and affirms the union with communal joy.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Song of Solomon 4:1-5:1, chapters 4 and 5. Poetic lines rendered as flowing prose within each verse; embedded speaker labels such as The Friends were treated as headings and not included in the verse text.
